executive_summary: Institutional investors grew more optimistic about the market's one-year outlook in June, while individual investors held steady. But beneath that headline confidence, crash worries lingered for both groups, and a striking gap opened in buy-on-dips faith — individual investors jumped sharply higher while institutional managers pulled back. Valuation skepticism remains widespread, though both groups edged up from May's readings.

key_findings.headline: Pros More Bullish, Individuals Steady
key_findings.interpretation: Nearly 86% of institutional investors expect higher prices a year from now, up from about 79% in May. Individual investors held essentially flat at around 72%, suggesting their medium-term optimism didn't budge.

key_findings.headline: Crash Fears Still Elevated
key_findings.interpretation: Fewer than half of institutional investors — and fewer than a quarter of individuals — feel confident a crash won't happen in the next six months. Both readings are roughly in line with May, meaning the unease that settled in last month hasn't lifted.

key_findings.headline: Individuals Embrace Quick Recoveries
key_findings.interpretation: Individual investors' buy-on-dips confidence surged to 75%, up from 56% in May, signaling growing faith that any sharp sell-off would bounce back fast. Institutional managers moved in the opposite direction, slipping to 50% — a notable divergence that could reflect different views on market liquidity or simply different recent experiences.

key_findings.headline: Most Still See Overvaluation
key_findings.interpretation: Roughly 56% of institutional investors and 60% of individuals continue to view the market as overpriced. Both groups ticked up from May, but a clear majority in each camp still sees valuations as stretched — though investors who subscribe to efficient-market thinking would note that the current price already incorporates all available information, making 'overvalued' a less meaningful label.

detailed_analysis:
The June data paints a picture of selective optimism. Institutional investors are the most confident they've been in three months that prices will be higher a year from now, and individual investors aren't far behind at 72%. That's a solid base of forward-looking bullishness. But it sits alongside persistent crash anxiety — like someone who plans a beach vacation but keeps checking the hurricane forecast.

The most eye-catching move this month is in buy-on-dips confidence among individual investors, which jumped from 56% to 75%. That's a big swing. One reading: everyday investors may be drawing on recent experience of quick market recoveries and extrapolating forward. Another possibility is that fresh cash on the sidelines is making people feel like any dip is a buying opportunity. Institutional managers, meanwhile, moved the other way — down to just 50% — which may suggest they see structural risks that could make a sell-off stickier than usual.

Valuation confidence remains low for both groups, though it bounced back somewhat from May's especially depressed readings. When fewer than half of respondents in either camp think the market is fairly priced, it signals broad unease about price levels. That said, this index has always been tricky to interpret. For investors who believe markets are reasonably efficient, the question of overvaluation is almost philosophical — the price is the price, and it reflects collective wisdom. For others, it's a flashing yellow light.

Taken together, the June numbers suggest a market mood that's hopeful but hedged. People expect gains, yet they worry about crashes and question whether current prices make sense. That kind of tension isn't unusual — in fact, it may be the normal state of a market climbing a wall of worry. Whether that worry is warranted or merely the background hum of investing is something only time will tell.
methodology: These indices come from the Yale/Shiller U.S. Stock Market Confidence Surveys, which have tracked investor sentiment since 1989. Each month, roughly 100 wealthy individual investors and 100 institutional investment managers answer the same standardized questions. The consistency of those questions over 35+ years is what makes the data meaningful — you can actually compare investor psychology across very different market environments. The four indices each measure something distinct: • 1-Year Confidence: The share who expect prices to be higher in 12 months. • Crash Confidence: The share who believe a crash in the next 6 months is very unlikely (under 10% probability). A low reading means most people think a crash is plausible. • Buy-on-Dips Confidence: The share who believe that after a 3% single-day market drop, prices would fully recover within two days. • Valuation Confidence: The share who do not believe the market is overvalued. Surveys were conducted semi-annually before 2001 and have been monthly since July 2001. Respondents rotate over time, but consistent characteristics — high income, investment experience — are maintained across the panel.
